answer.label: Not George Carlin — an unsigned 1959 card motto
answer.authorDates: Originator unrecorded · in print by 28 April 1959
answer.sourceLine: The sentence was already moving through American newspapers in April 1959, printed on unsigned novelty cards whose author was never recorded, and Quote Investigator ↗ states flatly that there is no substantive evidence George Carlin wrote or spoke it — the earliest credit to him it documents is a 2000 newspaper filler. The fan-run catalogue at georgecarlin.net ↗ is blunter still: the line turns up on none of his albums, books or HBO specials.

source.excerpt: Never underestimate the power of stupid people in large groups.
trail: 27 April 1930 — a partial version runs in Elsie Robinson’s syndicated column “Listen, World!” in the Danville Register: “Don’t underestimate the power of stupid, stubborn people with one idea.” Quote Investigator ↗

28 April 1959 — the full sentence appears in Will Jones’s “Day Brightener” item in the Minneapolis Morning Tribune, reported as the motto on cards being handed out by Eddie Schwartz. Within weeks it is reprinted around the country, including on cards circulated by members of the Elks. Quote Investigator ↗

23 April 2000 — the Ledger-Enquirer of Columbus, Georgia prints the line with George Carlin’s name attached. That is the earliest Carlin credit Quote Investigator documents, and it comes with no source of any kind. Quote Investigator ↗

Still unfound in his work — the unofficial fan archive georgecarlin.net files it under bogus quotations with the verdict “GEORGE CARLIN DID NOT say this,” noting it “doesn’t show up on any of his albums, books, or HBO specials.” georgecarlin.net ↗
source.excerptNote: The 1959 printings carry the sentence exactly like this — a free-standing motto with no speaker, no setting and no byline. That is the tell: Quote Investigator ↗ notes that a saying appearing on a card is a sign the originator was anonymous.

source.rightsNote: No author, publisher or first publication can be fixed for this wording: Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to an unsigned 1959 card whose originator is unknown, so quotle.info asserts no copyright status. It is emphatically not confirmed public domain — every documented printing is from 1959 or later, and an anonymous origin does not by itself put a text out of copyright.

author.name: George Carlin
author.kicker: The name on the card that isn’t his
author.heading: About the wrongly credited author
author.metaLine: 1937–2008 · American stand-up comedian, actor and author
author.bio: George Carlin (born 12 May 1937, died 22 June 2008) spent five decades in American comedy, from a start as a radio disc jockey in 1956 to fourteen HBO specials, five Grammy awards for best comedy album and a posthumous Mark Twain Prize ↗ in 2008. He genuinely did build routines around human stupidity and the dimness of crowds — which is precisely why unsigned cynicism drifts toward his name. This particular sentence is not his: it was in print before his first solo album, and it survives in none of his recorded or published work.

misattribution.heading: How Carlin’s name got attached
misattribution.intro: George Carlin is one of the internet’s most-forged bylines — a whole catalogue exists just to track the essays and one-liners falsely signed with his name. This one fits the pattern exactly: a sharp, cynical, crowd-hating line with no source, pinned to the most obvious cynic available.

items.why: Quote Investigator’s survey finds the earliest Carlin credit in the Ledger-Enquirer (Columbus, Georgia) on 23 April 2000, four decades after the sentence was already in national circulation, and concludes: “There is no substantive evidence that George Carlin wrote or spoke this statement.” Quote Investigator ↗

The fan-maintained bogus-quotes archive at georgecarlin.net — run by a self-described lifelong fan, not the estate — reports the line “doesn’t show up on any of his albums, books, or HBO specials.” georgecarlin.net ↗

The same archive notes it has “seen some other sources attribute it to Mark Twain, but I can’t find a source of where and when he might have said it.” Twain, like Carlin, is a default byline for unowned wit. georgecarlin.net ↗

AZQuotes prints it under Carlin’s name with no citation at all, and Goodreads carries it credited to him with over three thousand likes — while simultaneously tagging its own entry “attributed-no-source” and “misattributed-george-carlin.” The sentence is also the caption of Despair, Inc.’s Idiocy Demotivators poster. Goodreads ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it. It was an anonymous card motto in 1959, and Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that “the attribution to George Carlin is unsupported.” Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: A joke that travelled without a name
lead: Before the internet had forwarded emails, America had gag cards — printed one-liners handed round at clubs and lunch counters, passed on precisely because nobody owned them. That is what this sentence was in the spring of 1959: a motto on a card, reported in a Minneapolis newspaper column, reprinted within weeks in Montana, Cincinnati and Louisville, and signed by no one at any stage.

The chronology alone settles the Carlin question. When the line was already in national newspaper circulation in 1959, Carlin was a young radio man — he had started as a disc jockey in 1956, and his first solo comedy album, Take-Offs and Put-Ons, would not appear until 1966. His name only reaches the sentence in 2000.
context.detailsSummary: Why this one sticks to Carlin so well
detailsBody: Carlin did have a genuine, well-known routine on how stupid the average person is — which is exactly why the forgery works. The counterfeit sounds like him because it sits next to real material of his on the same theme, and once a line sounds like someone, the citation stops being asked for.

The 1930 precursor is worth noticing too. Elsie Robinson, a Hearst columnist whose “Listen, World!” ran to a mass daily readership, printed a partial version nearly three decades before the card — a reminder that the sentiment was in the air long before anyone got the wording into its final, quotable shape.
context.pull: A joke about crowds getting things wrong, kept alive for sixty-five years by a crowd getting it wrong.
